George
Be n s o n
From the very beginning,
the sound of the guitar
was always in my mind.
From the moment I heard
it, I knew that my life was
going to have something
to do with the guitar. I did
not know I was going to be
a player yet, but I loved the
sound.
                                    68
                           46




 As I grew older, I began to dabble with the guitar, to pick it up and try to pick things out. I would get so far, and
 then I would get stuck. I have found later that this is normal. Everybody goes through that on every instrument.
 To move forward, you have to take in more information, and look at things from different angles or from a dif-
 ferent point of view. So I started asking questions from the people whom I knew that had a certain mastery of the
 instrument.

 In my home town of Pittsburg, Pennsylvania, a lot of traveling groups would come through town and I always went up
 to the guitar player to ask if he could show me something. I was never too ashamed to ask. The George Benson you
 know today is a collection of all those people who took the time to show me what they knew, and the things I could
 hang on to did me a lot of good.

 From guitar books, which I was not a reader, I was more of a picture guy. But the demonstrations in the new books
 really helped a lot to show the correct fingerings for this, that, and the other. They showed how to make chords.
 The chords led me to the harmony, that helped me to become a better single line player.

       Peter Farrell
                                  68
                           46




          Peter Farrell was born in Sao Paulo, Brazil in 1981. Son of the singer Claudia Fier and the
          saxophone player Lino Simão. He began studying music at school very young with an early
          interest in flute & violin.

          Still very young, his mother introduced him to the jazz and classical worlds, giving him the
          opportunity to hear the music of George Benson, Antonio Carlos Jobim, Debussy, Ravel,
          Bach, Dori Caymmi, Toninho Horta, Bill Evans, Herbie Hancock and many others.

          However, just like every teenager, Peter loved rock’n’roll and at the age of 11 he asked his
          mother to take him to a guitar teacher. So he began studying guitar with José Walter, which
          gave him the first basic steps to rock and blues.

                              2019 © Jupiter Musical Group Ltd. All Rights Reserved
the George Benson Method                                                                                    4668




            One year later, the young boy was taken by his aunt Léa Freire and his uncle Sizão Mach-
            ado to a music conservatory called Groove, where he studied classical guitar, music
            theory, and jazz guitar with Leyve Miranda and Luis Cavalcante. In this period Peter
            started going deep into the music of George Benson and Wes Montgomery.

            Also in this period, Peter studied Brazilian music with the extraordinary guitar player Lula
            Galvão, and also piano with the great pianist and arranger Edmundo Cassis, who gave him
            a new vision about harmony.

            After many years of studying day and night, Peter started giving his first lessons and re-
            alized he had a great talent to teach and encourage others. Since then teaching has also
            become his passion.

            It did not take long until musicians all over the world started keeping their eyes on him
            because of his ability, technique and musicality. He was very advanced for an 18 year old
            boy. As a matter of fact, Peter was known in the musical scene as a prodigy since he was 14.

            Sometime later Peter was introduced to his idol and mentor George Benson. The connec-
            tion between them was instantaneous. The great Benson was amazed at Peter’s talent and
            how he had decoded many of his secrets. After a few months of friendship, Peter became
                                    68


            Mr. Benson’s private student and it has continued for the past 15 years.

            During the last six years Peter Farrell and George Benson have been dedicated to this col-
                           46




            lection of method books that they have created together: The George Benson Method.

            Peter Farrell has recorded and played with many great artists all over the world such as Jane
            Monheit, Brian McKnight, Eumir Deodato, Cesar Camargo Mariano, Romero Lubambo,
            Adam Rogers, and Didier Lockwood just to name a few.

How to use this book
Although a big part of this method is exclusively dedicated to the guitar, (because it refers to
chord construction and basic visualization of the guitar fretboard),it was created as a tool for all
instruments of all levels (beginner, intermediate and advanced). However, even if you are an
advanced player, make sure you know start at the beginning of the book, otherwise you will
easily get lost by the end of the book.


This method should be used as a dictionary of ideas and techniques. It's important to understand
that the way we approach the musical concepts, ideas and techniques presented here are unique
and cannot be found elsewhere.


Do not worry about learning everything from every chapter. You can go ahead as soon as you
understand the concepts. But always remember that you can come back to any chapter of any
book in order to learn more about a determined subject you want to study again.


Be careful when trying to learn too much at one time. Music is not about quantity but quality.


George and I have been working for many years on this giant collection of books to give you the
best we can and help those that love the guitar the way we do. We hope this method can open a
                               68


new world that was unknown until now. You have a treasure in your hands. It contains all the
knowledge that George Benson has been teaching me privately over the last 15 years.
                      46




Thanks a lot,


Peter Farrell

                                              Important device:
The patterns and scale visualizations in this book may have different time signatures in order to
help with the organization and visualization. Notice that depending on where and how we play
them on the fretboard, we will have more or less possibilities. Don’t let the time signatures
confuse you. Learn the ideas that you like the most and apply them where you feel they sound
the best. Give more attention to the single lines shown.

    Target Tones & Approach Tones
    What is a Target Tone? (also called Target Note)
    We de%ine Target Tones as the main notes of a melody. In other words, the starting notes,
    or ending notes. For example, the “C” major chord can have 3 target tones: C , E and G,
    and any other note we consider as passing notes also called approach notes. However, in
    addition to the chord tones, we can also set the chord tension notes from a determined
    scale as target tones, even if they do not belong to the chord itself.

    It is important to understand that we can only use chord tones or chord tension notes as
    target tones, but not avoid notes. The only exception would be when the avoid note
    becomes part of the chord. Therefore, let’s divide the target tones into two groups:


    a) Chord Target Tones

    b) Scale Target Tones (tension notes)
                                 68



    Types of ApproachTones:
                        46




    After understanding what a Target Tone is, let’s learn about what we call: Approaching
    Tones (passing notes), which are notes that circle the target tones. They are essential to
    get into the jazz improvisational world. We divide them into three different groups:


    1) Scale Tone Approach (Diatonic Approach)

    2 Chromatic Approach (simple, double and triple)

    3) Enclosure Approach

Scale Tone Approach
        68
   46




    2019 © Jupiter Musical Group Ltd. All Rights Reserved   2
    Scale Tone Approach (Diatonic Approach)
                                                                                                                                          4668




    This type of approaching tone is when you reach the target note by using scale notes
    immediately before or after it. When used over the major scale, it is called Diatonic
    Approach. However, as we are going to use other scales applying the same ideas, let’s call
    it simply “Scale Tone Approach” (ST). There are four types of ST: simple, double, triple and
    quadruple Scale Tone Approach.
    Notes used immediately before the target tone are called Ascending Scale Tone Approach,
    and notes used immediately after are called Descending Scale Tone Approach. See the
    examples below:


    Example 1: Scale Tone Approaches using the major scale notes

Chromatic Approach
        68
   46




    2019 © Jupiter Musical Group Ltd. All Rights Reserved   4
    Chromatic Approach                                                                          4668




    The chromatic approach is one of the oldest and most used concepts in the history of
    western music. This type of approach connects one note to another, using half steps
    between them. We have four chromatic approach possibilities, and each one of them can
    be ascending or descending.

    1) Simple Chromatic

    2) Double Chromatic

    3) Triple Chromatic

    4) Mixed Chromatic

    It is important to understand that depending on the chord, the possibilities of chromatic
    approaches can be different, because the distance from one note to another in each type
    of chord is different.

    Although it is one of the most used approaches in every style of improvisation,
    chromatics must be studied very carefully because the "borderline" between building a
    beautiful melody or a non-musical melody is very thin.
                                68


    1) Simple Chromatic Approach:
                       46




    Simple Chromatic Approach is when you approach a target tone by an ascending half
    step or by a descending half step. It is very important to mention that the simple
    chromatic approach is the only type of chromatic approach that does not require a source
    note to reach the target tone. The simple ascending chromatic approach usually sounds
    more familiar than the simple descending chromatic approach, since every ascending half
    step sounds like a leading one.
    • Examples:
    a) Simple Ascending Chromatic                     b) Simple Descending Chromatic

                       TT                                                           TT

    2) Double & Triple Chromatic Approach:
    The Double and the Triple Chromatic Approaches must always have a connection with a
    starting note and the ending note, otherwise they can change the melodic context, making
    the melody sound unpleasent or incorrect.

    Examples:

    a) Ascending             b) Descending                    c) Ascending            d) Descending
    Double Chromatic        Double Chromatic                 Triple Chromatic        Triple Chromatic

                                                                                           bœ œ bœ œ
    & bœ nœ œ                 & œ bœ œ                        & œ #œ œ œ               &
              TT                          TT                                 TT                   TT



    Very Important:
    The example below is a typical double chromatic approach example leading to a “C” note.
    However, it does not help us in anything, if we do not know the chord behind the notes.
    In other words, that melody can work or not.


    & bœ nœ œ
              TT
                                 68


    Let's look at the C6 chord for an example: if we were on the note "G" which is the perfect
    5th of "C", we could not apply the double chromatic (Bb, B) leading to “C” note, because it
                        46




    would create a melody belonging to C7 and not from C6. However, if we start on "A" we
    would have a beautiful melodic cell, but this time not using a double chromatic but a triple
    chromatic approach, which works perfect.



    & œ bœ nœ œ
                TT

    Summarizing, we must make sure we know the answer for the following questions before
    trying to apply more than one chromatic note to our melodic lines:
    1) Where am I ? ( What note of the chord am I on?)
    2) Where am I going? (What note of the chord am I going to ?)

     Mixed Chromatic
        Approach
            68

13      2019 © Jupiter Musical Group Ltd. All Rights Reserved
3) Mixed Chromatic Approach:
                                                                                                 4668




The Mixed Chromatic Approach is a combination of all types of chromatic approaches with
all types of Scale Tone Approaches, facilitating the melodic chaining between the chords,
and also transforming the common sound of sequential chromatic notes into hybrid
chromatic melodies, which will help us to get free from predictable melodies.

It is important to understand that the Mixed Chromatic Approach needs to have a source
note. In other words, it must start on a chord tone. Notice that in many cases it will contain
only scale notes, which may seem confusing because we could also call this a scale tone
approach.

In order to make this concept clearer we can say that you have to have at least one whole
step combined with one half step before landing on the target tone, independent from
containing only scale tones or mixing scale tones with chromatic notes out of the scale.



Breaking the “Rules”:
The most common way to play chromatics is to play chord tones on the down beats and
chromatic tones on the upbeats. We must be careful to not sound predictable by playing
predetermined rhythmic ideas. Jazz improvisation should sound free Flowing.
                             68


For many years the greatest jazz stars have been teaching us that improvisation is all about
rhythmic and melodic creativity. So why should we be stuck with a preset rhythm every
                    46




time? Remember that in the beginning preset "licks" are very important because we must
learn the "language"of improvisation.

As time goes by and we become more familiar with the "jazz language" we will be releasing
ourselves to play what we hear in our head and in the moment. This is what jazz is about, a
special moment that may not happen again. It is a kind of "musical kaleidoscope" that
shows us something different every time.

In theory, all the mixed chromatic approach possibilities can work ascending or descending.
However, when using double, triple or quadruple chromatics, we must be very careful in
order to not use melodies that might not work. As mentioned before, in many cases the best
option is to use scale tones only.

Enclosure Approach
        68
   46




    2019 © Jupiter Musical Group Ltd. All Rights Reserved   20
                                                                                                         4668




     This type of approaching tone is one of the most used in classical music and jazz, and in
     particular bebop. It consists of using notes that surround the chosen target tone,
     combining all the possibilities of approaching tones. However, we must understand that
     some enclosure approach possibilities may not work for some chords depending on the
     note we start on. See the two examples below:

     Ex 1: Wrong Option:                         1*In this example, we have an enclosure approach
     Scale Tone from Above                        leading to the octave of a Cmaj7 chord. However,
     Double Chr. from Below                       the melody does not work over this chord because
     Target Tone                                  of the "Bb" note, which makes the chord sound
                                                  dominant. This melody could work for chords

      Cmaj7
                                                  such: C7, Cm7 or Csus9 for example.



     & œ bœ nœ
     ⊗
                          œ
                         TT


     Ex 2: Great Option:                         2* In this case the melody created by
     Scale Tone from Below                       the enclosure works perfectly for Cmaj7.
     Double Chr. from Above
     Target Tone

         Cmaj7
                                   68


     & œ         œ bœ     œ
                          46




                         TT

     It is important to understand that depending on the scale or chord, the approaching possibilities
     for each note can vary, since some intervals give us more possibilities of approaching tones
     than others. To make the enclosure approach possibilities easier to understand, let's abbreviate
     the names of the approaching tones. See below:

     Options:
     a) ST = Scale Tone Approach                               e) DCh = Double Chromatic Approach
     b) DST = Double Scale Approach                            f) TCh = Triple Chromatic Approach
     c) TST = Triple Scale Approach                            g) Mix = Mixed Chromatic Approach
     d) SCh = Simple Chromatic Approach                        h) QCh = Quadruple Chromatic Approach

21                             2019 © Jupiter Musical Group Ltd. All Rights Reserved
Although we have learned many possibilities of enclosure approaches on the last page, it is
                                                                                                 4668




important to understand that the best options will always be those that have the closest
intervals between the approaching tones and the target tone, otherwise the enclosure
effect would almost disappear. In other words, we might have problems when using
Double, Triple or Quadruple Chromatic or Scale Tone approaches surrounding the target
tone at the same time. In order to clarify that explanation let's see a few examples below:

1) Notice that in letter “a” the enclosure creates a tritone between the 4th and the 7th
(F and B ), which makes that a wrong option for Cmaj7. However, if we use a similar
enclosure as in example “b”, the melody works great over the Cmaj7 chord.

Chapter 2

Dorian & Mixolydian Single Line Ideas
Dorian single lines are one of the most important subjects for those who want to learn
about improvisation, because they are related to the cadence II / V, and that is the reason
why we will not differenciate between dorian and mixolydian single lines. This type of
concept was very well developed in the bebop era by the great Charlie Parker, Dizzy
Gillespie, Bud Powell and many others.
In order to make it easy to understand, let’s name the chords. For example, if we have the
cadence Dm7 | G7 , we could play “D” dorian single lines over both chords. However, when
we have a single dominant 7th chord (G7 for example) we must be careful with the avoid
note "C", because it can make your melody sound weird or even incorrect. The only
exception is when the chord is a Gsus, so the “C” note will work with this chord as a
starting note or even an ending note. In other words, we dePinitely can use “D” dorian
ideas over G7, but without forgeting to emphasize the “B” note instead the “C” note.

We can use dorian ideas over any minor chord as a “possibility of color”. However, when
we have minor chords that do not belong to the harmonic Pield, there is no other option
than using dorian ideas, otherwise the melody will sound wrong.

Chord Superimposition Over Dm7 Dorian:
                             68


Before we start learning dorian single line ideas, let’s check some basic chord
superimposition possibilities to use over them. It’s very important to remember that the
                    46




dorian scale is a static scale, which means that it does not have any avoid note. Therefore,
we can play all the tetrads and triads from the harmonic Pield over a dorian chord. See
below:

• Tetrads: Cmaj7, Dm7, Em7, Fmaj7, G7, Am7, Bø
• Triads: C, Dm, Em, F, G, Am, B˚

Another important thing that we must know, is that we can add the major 7th to the
dorian scale, in order to make it more melodic. The reason we can do this, is because the
major 7th works as a leading tone to the root of the scale, thus creating the illusion of a
dominant 7th chord leading to a minor chord. So pay attention to the following single lines,
because we will use this concept frequently.


                         2019 © Jupiter Musical Group Ltd. All Rights Reserved             144
  From Major 7th Lines to Dorian lines:                                                                                                                                4668




  As we have learned previously, by combining Cmaj7 lines with Fmaj7 lines, we can build a
  beautiful D dorian line. So, it means that we already have thousands of dorian lines just
  adapting the major 7th lines to minor chords. Below we have some examples of Cmaj7
  ideas combined with Fmaj7 ideas. See the examples below:

      Dorian & Mixolydian
       Scale Possibilities


  Note:
                               68


  The following scale shapes will help you to better understand how to approach the dorian
  scale possibilities all over the guitar fretboard.
                      46




  The following scale examples are written in the key of Dm, but remember that everything
  related to the dorian mode is also related to the mixolydian mode because of the similarity
  between them. So we can use the following scales over Dm7 dorian or G7 mixolydian.

  It is important to understand that we use scales only to guide us through the guitar
  fretboard. When building melodic ideas, we should always mix scales, superimposed
  arppegios and chromatic tones, otherwise the improvisation will sound predictable.

Now that we have learned many tools and examples using scale arpeggios and other ideas
                                                                                                                             4668




in the key of “C” (Cmaj7 & Am7), it is time to understand how we can extend this concept
in order to start using it over different types of harmonic situations.

So let's start connecting scale/arpeggios from different keys in the same melodic idea. As
we know, we can use two types of scale arpeggios to build dorian single line ideas.
Therefore, for “Dm” dorian we can mix the scale arpeggios of Cmaj7 & Am7 and Fmaj7 &
Dm7.

However, we must understand that the Bive chord shapes related with the Bive zones will
appear in a different order depending on the key. For example, the chord shape
representing the 1st zone in the key of "C", represents the 4th zone in the key of F. The Birst
zone of a tonality will always be related to the closest chord shape from the Birst fret. In
order to better understand this concept, let’s look at the difference between the zones of
“C” major and “F” major.


• Cmaj7 "ive zones
 st

                      3fr.                5fr.         1        2   8fr.                        10fr.                12fr.
              2                                            34                                                    2
          3       4                                                             3       4                    3
                                         68



• Fmaj7 "ive zones
                             46

1 Zone: Fmaj7                2nd Zone: Dm7        3rd Zone: Dm7            4th Zone: Fmaj7              5th Zone: Dm7

      1           2                       3fr.                      5fr.                        8fr.                 10fr.

Note:
The scale/arpeggios should be understood as guiding melodies to help us, and not pre-set
melodies that cannot be changed. The most important thing is to know what we can play
melodically in each one of the Bive vertical guitar fretboard zones.

Connecting ideas:                                                                                     4668




In addition to helping us build more colorful single lines, the idea to connect scale/
arpeggios in different keys will help us start playing and thinking horizontally and not
only vertically. The =irst step to understand this is to study the connections between
neighboring zones (those that are close to each other). But before we begin to learn some
possibilities, let’s choose the “Cmaj7” zone chords to guide us (the Fmaj7 zones will be
related with one of the zones from Cmaj7).

Note:
The following examples are showing connections between two different zones. Basically
one from Cmaj7 and another from Fmaj7. However, we can connect two, three , four or
even =ive zones consecutively, thus creating a giant horizontal single line idea.

But remember that we should not rush into trying to learn all the possibilities right away.
The best way to learn is to practice the same ideas connecting only two zones everyday. As
time goes by and with more practice the larger connections will become more familiar.

         Additional
      Studies Using the
        Dorian Mode
             68
        46




179      2019 © Jupiter Musical Group Ltd. All Rights Reserved
In order to help us build more colorful single line ideas, let’s learn a new technique          4668




that deals with the connection between arpeggio degrees derived from the major scale.
The main idea is to connect two arpeggios that are close to each other using "neighboring
degrees".
Although this chapter speci?ically explores the dorian world, it is very important to
understand that all the melodic lines in this chapter can be used over any chord derived
form “C” major scale: Dm7 (Dorian), Em7 or Esus(b9) (Phrygian), Fmaj7 (Lydian), G7
(Mixolydian), Am7 (Aeolian), Bø (Locrian).


Arpeggio Degree Connection Options

          œ œ œ                                                          œ œ œ
& œ œ œ œ œ œ                                                  & œ œ œ œ œ œ

• ascending arpeggio                                          • ascending arpeggio
• go down to the next scale tone                              • go up to the next scale tone
• ascending arpeggio                                          • ascending arpeggio

Option B:                                                     Option D:
• ascending arpeggio                                          • ascending arpeggio
• go down to the next scale tone                              • go up to the next scale tone
• descending arpeggio                                         • descending arpeggio

       Melodic Patterns
           Using the
      Dorian Chord Family
              68
         46




197       2019 © Jupiter Musical Group Ltd. All Rights Reserved
The next series of pattern exercises are based on simple classical studies using chord                                                  4668




arpeggios derived from a "C" major scale. Remember that all the melodic or harmonic
material derived from a determined major scale works with all the chords from its chord
family. Therefore, in this chapter we will be using them to improve our melodic material
for the dorian mode, in this case "Dm7" ideas. Notice that we will have the same exercise
starting from the 6th, 5th, 4th and 3rd strings, making this a fantastic tool to improve our
horizontal visualization of the major scale. It is important to understand that we must
study this in two different ways:
1) Play the exercises very slowly in order to better visualize them on the fretboard. Keep
playing the same exercise in the same key until you feel comfortable with it.
2) Use the arpeggio sequence musically and not as an exercise. Therefore, we must combine
them with other melodic ideas we have learned before, creating new single lines.
Note: Remember that a fantastic device is to use odd rhythmic cells when we have even
notes, and use even rhythmic cells when we have odd notes. By doing this we take out the
“exercise feel”, making these arpeggio patterns sound more musical. But be careful, if we
insist on playing them too many times without combining them with other melodic ideas,
it can lead to sounding boring and predictable. So make sure to understand that these
patterns are fantastic tools when used musically.
Below is an example where we have "F" major chord family arpeggios played over a Gm7
dorian chord. However, pay attention, because there is a chromatic note before each chord
arppegio, making them sound more "colorful". This example was extracted from “Flute Song”,
                                                                                     Bb
which is the Nirst track of the album Benson & Farrell.

        Connecting Dorian
         Patterns & Other
          Melodic Ideas
Note:

As mentioned before, in order to make any melodic idea (pattern or lick) “become part” of
                            68


our playing, we must always sing the line while we play. As time goes by we will start
hearing what we will play before it happens, which means that we are really getting inside
                    46




the music and it is coming from within rather than from outside.

Of course we should also practice what we learn at fast tempos to be prepared for any
situation. Remember, playing fast tempos comes from playing everything slow and singing
every note.

Next we will have some dorian single line examples using the patterns we have just
learned combined with some other melodic tools such as arpeggios, scales and of course
approach tones.

There is no rule about how to best connect the melodic tools we have learned so far. But
remember to not over use any one melodic device. This can cause our playing to sound
predictable. This can especially happen with the overuse of predetermined patterns.

         Applying
    Dorian Single Lines
      Over Altered
              th
   Dominant 7 Chords
We can extend the use of the dorian single lines by applying them over dominant 7th
alterd chords. This is a very useful tool, especially to give the altered chord a different
                            68


“color” rather than using common scales over this type of chord. Let’s use a progression in
the key of Am as an example:
                    46




• || E7(alt) | Am7 ||

Now let’s consider E7(alt) chord as being E7(#9), which using the tritone substitution
become Bb7(13). However, Bb7(13) is a chord that is connected with Fm7, creating the
famous IIm7, V7. Summarizing we have:

E7(#9) = Bb7(13) = Fm7(9) or Abmaj7 (which is Fm major relative)
This idea came from the early bebop players who would apply the cadence IIm7, V7 over
any harmonic situation, which is absolutely fantastic. See some examples on the next pages:

  Harmonic Minor Single Line Ideas
      The most important characteristic from the harmonic minor scale is that it produces it's
      own dominant chord creating tension and resolution at the same time. But although we
      can use this scale in a static way over its chord family, we will use its melodies over
      harmonic situations where we have tension & resolution. Below are some harmonic
      examples in the key of "Cm" where we can use "C" harmornic minor lines.
      A very important and useful device for the harmonic minor lines is that we can also use
      the minor 7th, which is a note that is not derived from this scale but sounds great. The
      reason we can use both 7ths is because the harmonic minor came from the aeolian scale
      and both have the same harmonic function.
      Below we have a "C" harmonic minor line played over a G7/Cm7 cadence. However, always
      pay attention to the resolution note because we must always respect the ending chord,
      which in this case is Cm7, a non "C" harmonic minor scale chord. Actually, most of the
      time, the ending chord of a cadence V7/I will not be derived from the harmonic minor
      scale. We could for example use a "C" harmonic minor line over the cadence G7/Cmaj7, if
      we change the resolution note into one that Jits over Cmaj7. See below the example and
      the harmonic possibilities to use it:

  Guiding “C” Harmonic Minor Line
  (Note: pay attention because the line starts before the chord sequence starts)

Harmonic Minor & Ionian (#5)                                                                       4668




In order to better visualize the Harmonic Minor Scale, we will split the guitar fretboard
into 5 vertical zones based on guide chord shapes just like we did before with Ionian and
Aeolian. However, to understand what type of guide chord shapes we should use, we must
remember that every minor chord/scale has a relative major chord/scale or vice-versa. So
the relative from the Harmonic Minor chord/scale is what we call "Ionian (#5).
In order to avoid any confusion about the guide chord shapes when changing the scale modes,
let's use the key of "Cm" as an example and compare the chord/scales and their respective
relatives:
• Ionian & Aeolian = Ebmaj7 & Cm7
• Ionian (#5) & Harmonic Minor = Ebmaj7(#5) & Cm(maj7)
For the following harmonic minor examples we have chosen the key of "Cm" as well. See
below

       Diminished Chords
        Derived from the
      Harmonic Minor Scale

                                           Attention:
                                 68


      Although we were using the harmonic minor scale in the key of "Am" previously, from
      now on let's use it in the key of "Cm". It is important to understand that we are changing
                        46




      the key of the scale for the next exercises on purpose. This way you will be able to check
      if you really understand the concepts and how the guiding chords work.




245                          2019 © Jupiter Musical Group Ltd. All Rights Reserved
Ascending Diminished Chord Shapes:                                                                            4668




On the VII degree of the harmonic minor scale we have a diminished chord (in the case of
“C” harmonic minor we have "B" diminished). As we know, every diminished chord is
symmetrical, so B˚ will provide us three more equal chords: D˚, F˚ and Ab˚. However, all of
them are what we call fake diminished chords, because they are G7(b9) [V7] without the
root note. See below the relationship between B˚ and its chord family (D˚, F˚ and Ab˚) with
G7.
a) B˚ : B, D, F, Ab ------- (major 3rd, perf 5th, minor 7th and =lat 9th of "G")
b) D˚ : D, F, Ab, B ------- (perf 5th, minor 7th, =lat 9th and major 3rd of "G")
c) F˚ : F, Ab, B, D (enharmonic) --- (minor 7th, =lat 9th, major 3rd and perf 5th of "G")
d) Ab˚ : Ab, B, D, F (enharmonic) - (=lat 9th, major 3rd, perf 5th and minor 7th of "G")

In order to help us better visualize the diminished arpeggio shapes on the guitar fretboard,
let’s learn every possibility starting from each string (6th, 5th, 4th, 3rd, 2nd):

  After learning the diminished chord shape possibilities for each string, now is time to
  organize them using the 8ive fretboard zones. In other words, each guiding chord derived
  from each zone will be related with the diminished chords that are close to it. Remember
  that the guiding chords for the harmonic minor scale are different from the ones derived
  from the major scale. Therefore, for “C” harmonic minor scale we have the chords Cm(maj7)
  and Eb+maj7 ( I and bIII degree).

single line ideas using the diminished chord as demonstrated on the following pages.

Chromatic Illusion                                                                                                                                              4668




Another device that can help us build more colorful melodic lines is to simply play
chromatics between the arpeggiated notes derived from a determined scale. By doing this
we create the illusion of playing more than one scale at the same time. (Note: Most often
we will only use simple ascending chromatic approaches over the diminished arpeggios.
Descending chromatic approaches work differently and we will cover them next.)
Below we have some examples using the simple chromatic approach between the
diminished chord arpeggios derived from the “C” Harmonic Minor scale (B˚, D˚, F˚, Ab˚).
Notice that the melodies seem to be a combination of two different scales, sometimes "C"
Hamonic Minor scale mixed with “C” Dominant Diminished scale, and other times "C"
Hamonic Minor scale mixed with “C” Altered scale (Note: We will cover the Dominant
Diminished scale in the next chapters).
Ch= Chromatic

  About the Simple Descending Chromatics over Diminished chords

  As mentioned before, the simple descending chromatics might not work when used over
  diminished chords derived from the harmonic minor scale. But it is important to really
  understand the reason why we use or don't use determined notes in some speci=ic
  situations.

  For example, the dorian scale is static, which means it does not have harmonic motion,
  only one chord is enough. On the other hand, active scales such as aeolian, ionian and the
  harmonic minor scale need harmonic motion to sound correct. Let's use two speci=ic
  scales:


  Dorian vs Aeolian


  The main diference between these two scales is the 6th degree, which de=ines whether a
  scale is static or active. For example, when we have a single line that uses a =lat 6th, we can
  conclude the line was built from an active scale, and should be played when we have
  harmonic motion (cadences). Let's use the key of "Cm" to better understand the idea. If we
  have the cadence G7, Cm7, we cannot use the "A" note (major 6th) to build single lines,
  because this note is derived from the dorian scale and cannot be played over any cadence.

  However, there are some exceptions. For example, over the cadence G7, Cm7 we could play
  dorian ideas over the Cm7, but it still is a dangerous option because depending where we
                                       68


  use the dorian scale, the whole single line might sound completely wrong.

  It is important to remember that this chapter talks about the harmonic minor scale which
                                 46




  creates it own dominant. In other words, we are talking about melodies that work over
  cadences ( in the case of “C” harmonic minor scale, the B˚ works as a G7). Below is a
  very didatic explanation about simple ascending and simple descending chromatic notes
  used over B˚ chord (VII degree from “C” harmonic minor scale):


     Works <ine, because the        Works <ine, because the       Can work as a blue note        Does not work at all in any
    chromatic note belongs to      chromatic note belongs to    however, sometimes it might    situation, because the”A” note
  the “C” harmonic minor scale   the “C” harmonic minor scale       sound not melodic         is derived from “D” dorian that
                                                                                              cannot be played over cadence

 Augmented Chords
  Derived from the
Harmonic Minor Scale

     2019 © Jupiter Musical Group Ltd. All Rights Reserved   280
  Ascending Augmented Chord Shapes:                                                                       4668




  In addition to the diminished chords, the harmonic minor scale can give us an
  augmemented chord which is also symmetric, giving us three equal augmented chords.
  In the case of “C” harmonic minor we have: G+, B+, D#+ (or Eb+). See below the
  relationship between these chords with G7:

  a) G+: G, B, D# ------- (Root , major 3rd , augmented 5th of "G")
  b) B+: B, D#, G ------- (major 3rd, augmented 5th, Root of "G")
  c) D#+: Eb, G, B (enharmonic) ------- (minor 6th, Root, major 3rd of "G")

  Below some examples using these augmented chords:

  Descending Augmented Chord Shapes:                                                                                                          4668




  In order to keep the alternate picking when going from the higher notes to the lower notes,
  the descending augmented chord shapes will be played horizontally, and for this reason we
  will have only one shape possibility per string.

  Of course we could use the sweep technique to give us more possibilities, but as
  mentioned before, the George Benson picking technique works much better when we play
  horizontal ideas (mainly when we have a melodic line going from the high to low). Below
  are some possibilities of B augmented chord arpeggios for each string:

Adding the Harmonic
 Minor Chord Family
over the Single Lines
         68
    46




     2019 © Jupiter Musical Group Ltd. All Rights Reserved   308
  Aside from the symmetric chords, we can use the triads and tetrads from "C" harmonic                                           4668




  minor scale to create melodies over G7 leading to Cm7. However, be careful when using
  the root of the Cm (maj7), because it can sound weird, making the whole line sound
  incorrect. So the best thing to do it is to forget the root for now. See the example below:
  Dø               Eb+(maj7)                          Fm7               G7              Abmaj7
  II                  III                              IV                V                V
  Note: Some degrees from the harmonic minor scale can contain more than one type of tetrad. It
  will help us build more colorful melodies using this scale. Pay attention and be careful to not rest
  on the "C" note because it will make the feeling of leading almost disappear. We can use the triads
  and tetrads that contain the "C" note (Dø, Fm7, Abmaj7) only as passing chords in a melody going
  from G7 leading to Cm7.
  • V degree: can also be used as G+7
  • IV degree: can also be used as Fø, F˚ (Ab˚, B˚, D˚)
  • bVI degree: can also be used as Abm(maj7), Ab˚(maj7)
      We can use the triads and tetrads that contain the "C" note (Dø, Fm7, Abmaj7) only as
      passing chords in a melody going from G7 leading to Cm7.
      In order to better visualize the triads and tetrads derived from “C” harmonic minor scale
      all over the guitar fretboard, let’s also use the Hive fretboard zones with their related
      guiding chords. In the key of “Cm” we have: Cm(maj7) and Eb+maj7. See below:

            Additional
         Studies Using the
       Harmonic Minor Scale
                                            Attention:
      Just as we did before with the dorian mode, it is time to start building single lines
      connecting the harmonic minor scale and its “neighboring” degrees.

      All the melodic lines in this chapter can be used over any IIø, V7, Im7 cadence and
      any chord sequences derived from it just as we have learned previously with
      harmonic regions. In order to refresh our memory, below are some examples of
      similar chord sequences:


      a) Dø, G7, Cm7
                                68


      b) Abmaj7, Cm7
      c) G7, Cm7
                       46




      d) Fm,7 G7, Cm7
      e) Abmaj7, Fm7, Cm7
      f) Fm7, Bb7, Cm7


      It is important to remember that some harmonic minor scale degrees should be
      changed in order to build a better melodic line. For example if we have a “C” harmonic
      minor scale, we shoud be able to use it over the cadence Dø, G7, Cm7. However, the
      “C” note contained in some degrees of this scale can make our melodic line sound
      incorrect, mainly over G7 chord. The "C" note will clash with the "B" note in the G7
      chord. See below and let’s refresh our memory:


335                         2019 © Jupiter Musical Group Ltd. All Rights Reserved
• First dregree = Cm(maj7): can be replaced by B+ or B+maj7 (note: the Bb note can be            4668




  incorporated to the harmonic minor scale as we have learned before)
• Second dregree = Dø: can be replaced by D˚
• Fourth dregree = Fm7: can be replaced by F˚, or Fø
• Fifth dregree = G7: can be replaced by G+7
• Sixth dregree = Abmaj7: can be replaced by Abm(maj7) or Ab˚(maj7)


Arpeggio Degree Connection Options
